title: EVOO Minor Polar Compounds in CKD Patients (Noce et al. 2021)
sample_size: n=40 (CKD patients)
finding: High-polyphenol EVOO (40mL/day, 9wk): CRP 4.2→2.8 mg/L (p=0.0011); ESR 41.6→35.1 mm/h (p=0.0005); IL-6 85.2→34.3 pg/mL (p=0.0321). CRP reduction persisted 2 months post-washout.
limitations: Small n; CKD-specific population; results may not generalise to healthy adults

title: Cardiovascular Benefits of EVOO (Esposito & Mandalà 2025)
sample_size: Multiple (PREDIMED n=7447; Harvard n=99000)
finding: PREDIMED: 30% reduction in major CV events with EVOO-supplemented MedDiet. Harvard cohort (24yr): >=0.5 tbsp/day linked to 15% lower CVD risk, 21% lower CHD risk.
limitations: Hard to isolate EVOO-specific effects from full MedDiet; polyphenol bioavailability variable
health_goal_tags: Cardiovascular health; Inflammation & immunity; Longevity & ageing

title: Cognitive and Cerebral Blood Flow Effects of Greek Mountain Tea (Wightman et al. 2018)
sample_size: n=155 (50–70yr, male and female)
finding: 950mg/day × 28d: significantly fewer RVIP false alarms (Day 28, p<0.05); state anxiety reduced vs placebo and Ginkgo control (Day 28); increased prefrontal cortex oxygenated haemoglobin (HbO) and oxygen saturation (Ox%) during cognitive tasks (Day 1, both doses).
limitations: Acute and chronic mechanisms appear to differ (CBF vs anxiety reduction); Ginkgo active control limits clean placebo comparison; no biomarker verification of polyphenol absorption

title: SidTea+ Effect on Physiological Profile and Metabolic Health in Healthy Adults (Papanikolaou et al. 2024)
sample_size: n=28 (healthy adults)
finding: 1500mg/day × 4wk: systolic BP −10.8 mmHg (p<0.05); mean arterial pressure −4.5 mmHg; resting HR −3.1 bpm; VO₂max +1.1 mL/kg/min; γ-GT −3.7 U/L; SGPT −3.3 U/L; total antioxidant capacity increased (p<0.001); lipid peroxidation decreased (p<0.05).
limitations: Small n=28; short duration (4 weeks); healthy adults only — clinical relevance for disease populations unclear
health_goal_tags: Cardiovascular health; Energy & metabolism; Inflammation & immunity

title: Purslane Supplementation on Inflammation and Antioxidant Markers in Rheumatoid Arthritis (Karimi et al. 2024)
sample_size: n=86 (77 completed; RA patients, 20–79yr, 12wk)
finding: 1000mg/day: pain VAS 53.38→26.25 (p≤0.001); DAS28 5.17→3.48 (p≤0.001); swollen joint count 4.42→1.60 (p≤0.001); tender joint count 8.20→2.78 (p≤0.001); hs-CRP reduced (p≤0.001); TNF-α 2.885→2.330 (p=0.046); ESR 36.52→26.70 mm/h (p=0.007); SOD increased (p=0.037); total antioxidant capacity increased (p≤0.001).
limitations: RA-specific population; results may not generalise to healthy adults; mechanism of bioactive action not fully characterised in the paper

title: Purslane on CRP and Glycaemic and Lipid Control in Type 2 Diabetes: Meta-Analysis of RCTs (Guo et al. 2024)
sample_size: Multiple RCTs in T2DM patients
finding: Purslane supplementation: FBG WMD −15.01 mg/dL (p=0.004); total cholesterol WMD −17.75 mg/dL (p<0.001); TG WMD −21.30 mg/dL (p<0.001); LDL-C WMD −6.10 mg/dL (p<0.001); HDL-C WMD +6.17 mg/dL (p<0.001); CRP WMD −1.44 mg/L (p<0.001). HbA1c, insulin, and HOMA-IR not significantly changed.
limitations: T2DM-specific population; variability across pooled trials; HbA1c and insulin resistance not significantly improved; authors note high-quality trials still needed
health_goal_tags: Energy & metabolism; Cardiovascular health; Inflammation & immunity

title: Portulaca oleracea Extract on Functional Constipation: A Randomized Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Trial (Bang et al. 2022)
sample_size: n=60 (functional constipation; Rome IV criteria; 8wk)
finding: P. oleracea extract: complete spontaneous bowel movement significantly improved vs placebo (p=0.003); colonic transit time 44.5→33.7h (p=0.04); PAC-QOL and PAC-SYM scores improved (p<0.05). No significant difference in Bristol Stool Form Scale between groups.
limitations: Constipation-specific population; results may not generalise to healthy gut; no biomarker data; mechanism not characterised

title: Cheese Consumption and Multiple Health Outcomes: Umbrella Review and Updated Meta-Analysis (Zhang et al. 2023)
sample_size: Multiple prospective studies; 47 health outcomes; evidence extrapolated to hard cheese category including Graviera
finding: Cheese consumption inversely associated with: all-cause mortality (RR=0.95; 95% CI 0.92–0.99); cardiovascular mortality (RR=0.93); incident CVD (RR=0.92); CHD (RR=0.92); stroke (RR=0.93); T2DM (RR=0.93); total fracture (RR=0.90); dementia (RR=0.81). Null associations found for other outcomes. Moderate NutriGrade evidence quality.
limitations: All observational prospective studies — no RCTs; evidence applies to generic cheese category extrapolated to Graviera specifically; dietary confounding from overall patterns possible
health_goal_tags: Cardiovascular health; Longevity & ageing; Mental clarity & stress; Energy & metabolism

title: Global Analysis of Dairy Consumption and Incident Cardiovascular Disease (Zhuang et al. 2025)
sample_size: UK Biobank + China Kadoorie Biobank (large population cohorts) + updated meta-analysis; evidence extrapolated to hard cheese category including Graviera
finding: Cheese specifically associated with reduced CVD risk in UK Biobank. Meta-analysis: total dairy consumption associated with −3.7% CVD risk and −6% stroke risk. Inverse associations with CVD incidence observed specifically for cheese and low-fat dairy products.
limitations: Observational cohort design; Chinese cohort showed divergent results from British cohort (possible dietary-context effects); evidence extrapolated from generic cheese category to Graviera

title: Probiotic Features of Lactic Acid Bacteria from Traditional Greek Dairy Products Including Graviera (Zoumpopoulou et al. 2018)
sample_size: Not applicable (in vitro cell study; strains isolated directly from Graviera and 6 other Greek artisanal cheeses)
finding: L. plantarum ACA-DC 2640 and ACA-DC 4039 isolated directly from Graviera showed highest gut epithelial adhesion (Caco-2 and HT-29 cells). L. plantarum ACA-DC 2640 showed anti-inflammatory modulation (IL-10 mRNA upregulation) in THP-1 macrophages. Milk cell-free supernatants of both L. plantarum strains showed strong ACE-inhibitory activity (antihypertensive potential).
limitations: In vitro study only — results not validated in human trials; probiotic strains not yet tested as dietary supplements in humans; findings specific to artisanal Graviera (not industrially produced)
health_goal_tags: Gut health & digestion; Inflammation & immunity; Cardiovascular health

title: Assessment of thyme honey oral gel for the prevention of adriamycin and cyclophosphamide chemotherapy-induced oral mucositis in patients with breast cancer (Jahanbani Mazraeh et al. 2023)
sample_size: n=110 (breast cancer patients receiving AC chemotherapy)
finding: Thyme honey oral gel (applied 2–4×/day) vs standard oral hygiene: reduced incidence of grade ≥2 oral mucositis (OR 0.33; p=0.030); shortened OM duration by 3.36 days (95% CI −5.50 to −1.22; p=0.037); delayed onset of grade ≥2 OM (OR 0.28; p=0.017).
limitations: Specialist oncology population limits generalisability to healthy adults; oral gel formulation not equivalent to dietary honey consumption; single-centre Iranian study; no mechanistic biomarker data; no dose–response data

title: Synergistic Beneficial Effect of Thyme Honey and Olive Oil against Diabetes and Its Complications Induced by Alloxan in Wistar Rats (Lafraxo et al. 2021)
sample_size: n=42 Wistar rats (alloxan-induced T1DM model)
finding: Combined thyme honey (2 g/kg) + olive oil (10 mL/kg) for 30 days: blood glucose 318→159 mg/dL; TC, TG, LDL normalised (p<0.001); hepatic enzymes (ALT, AST) and kidney markers (creatinine, urea) normalised; catalase, GSH, GPx increased; MDA decreased across liver, pancreas, and kidney tissue; near-normal histological recovery of pancreatic islets, hepatocytes, and renal tubules. Thyme honey polyphenol content: 192.82 ± 15.24 mg/100g; DPPH IC50 15.37 mg/mL.
limitations: Animal study only — alloxan T1DM model does not replicate human T2DM physiology; combination treatment prevents attribution of effects to thyme honey alone vs EVOO; no human-equivalent dose established; no honey-only control arm

title: Antibacterial Activity and Prebiotic Properties of Six Types of Lamiaceae Honey (Nazzaro et al. 2024)
sample_size: Not applicable (in vitro; bacterial pathogens and probiotic strains)
finding: Thyme honey: inhibited mature S. aureus biofilms by 80.32% and A. baumannii biofilms by 50.11% at 8 μg/mL; MIC against A. baumannii and E. coli 38 μg/mL; immature S. aureus biofilm inhibition 31.52%. Prebiotic activity: stimulated L. rhamnosus growth +11.48%; L. rhamnosus supernatant OHRS (hydroxyl radical scavenging) 65.8% — strongest radical scavenging among tested combinations.
limitations: In vitro only — antimicrobial concentrations may not be achievable via dietary consumption; comparative study of 6 Lamiaceae honeys, thyme honey not always the top performer; no Cretan-origin honey specifically tested; no human or animal validation

title: Beneficial Effects of Sideritis scardica and Cichorium spinosum against Amyloidogenic Pathway and Tau Misprocessing in Alzheimer's Disease Neuronal Cell Culture Models (Chalatsa et al. 2018)
sample_size: Not applicable (in vitro; SH-SY5Y-AβPP and PC12-htau neuronal AD cell culture models)
finding: C. spinosum extract significantly reduced total tau protein and tau hyperphosphorylation; decreased activation of GSK3β, ERK1, and ERK2 kinases (key tau phosphorylation drivers); promoted non-amyloidogenic α-secretase Aβ-APP processing — blocking both major AD pathological hallmarks (tau tangles and amyloid plaques) simultaneously.
limitations: In vitro neuronal cell culture only — not validated in animal or human models; study jointly reports C. spinosum and S. scardica without isolating individual contributions; specific active compounds not identified; specific quantitative magnitudes not available from published abstract

title: Extracts from Mediterranean Food Plants including Cichorium spinosum Enhanced GSH Levels and Reduced ROS in Human Endothelial Cells (Stagos et al. 2018)
sample_size: Not applicable (in vitro; EA.hy926 human endothelial cell line)
finding: C. spinosum extract (TPC 117 mg GAE/g dw; ABTS IC50 28.0 ± 3.1 μg/ml; O₂•⁻ IC50 21.0 ± 1.4 μg/ml): increased intracellular GSH by 10.5% at 50 μg/ml; reduced intracellular ROS by 15.6% at 100 μg/ml in human endothelial cells. Key polyphenols identified: cichoric acid, caftaric acid, caffeoylquinic acid isomers, quercetin, luteolin. Note: Nrf2 gene induction was observed for C. intybus (a related species) but not specifically tested for C. spinosum.
limitations: In vitro only; C. spinosum showed more modest effects than other plants in the same study; specific dietary concentrations vs cell culture concentrations not established; multi-plant comparative study

title: Phytochemical Analysis and Antioxidant Potential of the Phytonutrient-Rich Decoction of Cichorium spinosum and C. intybus (Brieudes et al. 2016)
sample_size: Not applicable (in vitro; human fibroblast cell line)
finding: Traditional Cretan C. spinosum decoction: non-cytotoxic in human fibroblasts; significantly reduced intracellular ROS; major antioxidants characterised as cichoric acid and caftaric acid by UHPLC-HRMS; isolated a sulfoconjugate sesquiterpene lactone (8-deacetylmatricarin-8-O-sulphate) present only in Cretan C. spinosum — not found in C. intybus or other chicory varieties; authors describe effective dose as 'comparable to ingestion of a phytomedical preparation of antioxidants'.
limitations: In vitro only; specific ROS reduction magnitude not disclosed in abstract (full text paywalled); compound bioavailability from dietary consumption not established; traditional 'liver detoxifying' claim not directly tested

title: Phytochemical Composition of the Decoctions of Greek Edible Greens (Chórta) and Evaluation of Antioxidant and Cytotoxic Properties (Mikropoulou et al. 2018)
sample_size: Not applicable (in vitro; human fibroblast and tumour cell lines)
finding: C. spinosum decoction DPPH IC50 ~15 μg/mL; phenolic profile dominated by cichoric acid, caftaric acid derivatives, quercetin-3-O-glucuronide, luteolin glucuronides, and sesquiterpene lactones (lactupicrin; 8-deacetylmatricarin-8-O-sulphate); non-cytotoxic to human cells; no differential cytotoxicity against tumour cell lines (differential cytotoxicity found only in C. endivia, not C. spinosum).
limitations: Primarily a characterisation study — no specific health outcome beyond antioxidant activity and safety for C. spinosum; multi-plant comparative study across Greek chórta species; differential cytotoxicity reported in abstract belongs to C. endivia not C. spinosum

title: A Metabolomic Approach to Investigate the Effect of Phytonutrients on Proteostasis and Metabolic Pathways in Drosophila melanogaster (Mikropoulou et al. 2024)
sample_size: Drosophila melanogaster (invertebrate model)
finding: C. spinosum phytonutrient extract modulated the proteostasis network and metabolism of young Drosophila; untargeted metabolomics (C18 UPLC-ESI-Orbitrap-HRMS/MS) detected altered lysophosphatidylcholines, acylcarnitines, and phosphatidylethanolamines; distinct sex-based metabolomic signatures (PLS-DA separation by sex); extract modulated lipid metabolism, amino acid metabolism, and proteostasis-related pathways.
limitations: Invertebrate model (Drosophila) — limited translational relevance to human physiology; study primarily methodological (validating Drosophila as a platform for phytonutrient research); no specific quantitative health outcome data; no comparison with control diet outcomes published in abstract

title: Cooking Oil/Fat Consumption and Cardiometabolic Mortality (Zhang et al., 2021)
sample_size: n=521,120 (NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study; US adults aged 50–71; median 16-year follow-up; 129,328 deaths recorded)
finding: Olive oil intake associated with lower cardiometabolic mortality: HR 0.96 (95% CI 0.92–0.99) per 1-tbsp/day increment. Replacing butter or margarine with equal amounts of olive oil was associated with lower all-cause mortality and mortality from CVD, diabetes, cancer, respiratory disease, and Alzheimer's disease. Butter consumption positively associated with cancer mortality.
limitations: Observational design — cannot establish causation; self-reported dietary data via FFQ; cohort predominantly US adults, lower baseline olive oil consumption than Mediterranean populations; EVOO vs standard olive oil not distinguished

title: Mediterranean Diet with EVOO Improves Cognitive Function: PREDIMED-NAVARRA RCT (Martínez-Lapiscina et al., 2013)
sample_size: n=522 (high vascular risk; mean age 74.6yr; 6.5-year follow-up; PREDIMED-NAVARRA sub-study)
finding: MedDiet+EVOO vs low-fat control: MMSE score +0.62 (95% CI +0.18 to +1.05; p=0.005); Clock Drawing Test +0.51 (95% CI +0.20 to +0.82; p=0.001). Results adjusted for sex, age, education, ApoE genotype, family history of dementia, smoking, BMI, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, diabetes, alcohol, and energy intake. MedDiet+Nuts group also showed improvement vs control.
limitations: EVOO supplemented as part of full MedDiet — EVOO-specific contribution cannot be isolated; participants at high cardiovascular risk not general population; MMSE and CDT are global cognitive screens; cognitive outcomes were secondary endpoints in the parent PREDIMED trial

title: Oleracein E from Portulaca oleracea Improves Cognition and Survival in Senescent Mice (Wang et al. 2016)
sample_size: n=42 senescent Kunming mice (D-galactose/NaNO2 model; 8-week treatment)
finding: Oleracein E — a pyrrolidone/tetrahydroisoquinoline compound isolated from purslane — at 15 mg/kg/day for 8 weeks: significantly prolonged lifespan vs untreated senescent mice (p<0.05); improved spatial memory in Morris water maze to near-normal levels; restored brain antioxidant biomarkers (GSH, T-AOC, SOD); inhibited hippocampal neuronal apoptosis (Bcl-2 upregulated; Bax and Caspase-3 downregulated). Effect comparable to the nootropic piracetam (400 mg/kg).
limitations: Animal model only — D-galactose/NaNO2 model does not replicate human neurodegeneration; oleracein E requires extraction and is not directly equivalent to dietary purslane; dose-to-food equivalence not established

title: Virgin Olive Oil Polyphenols Modulate Gut Microbiota and ox-LDL in Hypercholesterolaemic Adults (Martin-Pelaez et al. 2015)
sample_size: n=12 (hypercholesterolaemic adults; randomised double-blind crossover; 3 arms x 3-week periods with 2-week washouts)
finding: PC-enriched VOO + thyme phenolics (FVOOT; 500 mg PC/kg; 25 mL/day; 3 weeks): significantly increased faecal bifidobacteria vs standard VOO (p<0.05); decreased serum ox-LDL vs pre-intervention; increased protocatechuic acid (key hydroxytyrosol metabolite). PC-enriched VOO alone increased hydroxytyrosol metabolites in faeces and blood, confirming polyphenol absorption and gut metabolism.
limitations: Very small n=12; crossover design; most effective arm combined olive + thyme phenolics — contributions cannot be separated; polyphenol concentration (500 mg/kg) higher than typical EVOO;

title: Antimicrobial, Antioxidant and Antiproliferative Activity of Origanum dictamnus Essential Oil (Mitropoulou et al. 2015)
sample_size: Not applicable (in vitro; bacterial/fungal pathogens; HepG2 cell line)
finding: Dittany EO (carvacrol 52.2%; gamma-terpinene 8.4%; p-cymene 6.1%): inhibited S. aureus, S. epidermidis, E. coli, L. monocytogenes, Salmonella Enteritidis/Typhimurium, S. cerevisiae, A. niger; DPPH antioxidant IC50 0.045 +/- 0.0042% v/v; antiproliferative against HepG2 hepatoma cells EC50 0.0069 +/- 0.00014% (primarily via carvacrol membrane disruption).
limitations: In vitro only — concentrations for pathogen inhibition may not be achievable via dietary herbal infusion; no pharmacokinetic data for human consumption

title: Origanum dictamnus as a Functional Food Ingredient: Gut Motility Modulation and Phytochemical Characterisation (Paloukopoulou et al. 2026)
sample_size: Not applicable (ex vivo isolated rabbit jejunum and colon; organ bath model)
finding: Traditional dittany infusion demonstrated spasmolytic activity in isolated rabbit intestinal tissue — modulated phasic and tonic contractions in jejunum and colon; benchmarked against scopolamine; receptor inhibition assays suggest partial parasympathomimetic mechanism. Four novel flavone glycosides (luteolin/apigenin caffeoyl/feruloyl glucuronopyranoside conjugates) characterised for the first time by NMR and HPLC-PDA-MS. Authors conclude findings scientifically support traditional Cretan digestive use.
limitations: Ex vivo isolated organ — does not replicate systemic absorption in a living organism; rabbit tissue may not quantitatively predict human gut response; no dose-to-cup equivalence established

title: Enzyme Inhibitory Activity of Origanum dictamnus Essential Oil: Cholinesterases, alpha-Glucosidase and Lipase (Amato et al. 2025)
sample_size: Not applicable (in vitro enzymatic assays; in silico molecular docking)
finding: Dittany EO inhibited AChE (mixed inhibition) and BuChE (competitive inhibition) — enzymes central to Alzheimer's disease cholinergic pathology; inhibited alpha-glucosidase (mixed) — relevant to post-prandial glycaemic control; inhibited lipase (mixed) — relevant to fat metabolism; inhibited tyrosinase (non-competitive). Molecular docking confirmed carvacrol and p-cymene bind AChE and BuChE active sites.
limitations: In vitro/in silico only — inhibitory concentrations not validated in animal or human models; essential oil bioavailability from herbal infusion not established; carvacrol partially volatilises during brewing

title: Carob Pulp Preparation Rich in Insoluble Fibre Lowers Total and LDL Cholesterol in Hypercholesterolaemic Patients (Zunft et al. 2003)
sample_size: n=58 (hypercholesterolaemic volunteers; randomised double-blind placebo-controlled parallel-arm; 6-week intervention)
finding: Carob fibre 15 g/day (delivered in fortified bread and fruitbar): LDL cholesterol −10.5 ± 2.2% (p=0.010) vs placebo; LDL:HDL ratio marginally decreased −7.9 ± 2.2% (p=0.058); triglycerides in females −11.3 ± 4.5% (p=0.030). Lipid-lowering effects were more pronounced in females than males. Total cholesterol and HDL not significantly changed.
limitations: Hypercholesterolaemic population only — results may not generalise to healthy adults; carob fibre was delivered in a fortified food matrix; sex differences in response limit generalisability

title: Insoluble Carob Fibre Rich in Polyphenols Lowers Total and LDL Cholesterol in Hypercholesterolaemic Subjects (Ruiz-Roso et al. 2010)
sample_size: n=88 (hypercholesterolaemic volunteers; double-blind randomised placebo-controlled; 4 weeks)
finding: Polyphenol-rich insoluble carob fibre (8 g/day in two doses): total cholesterol −17.8 ± 6.1% (p<0.05); LDL cholesterol −22.5 ± 8.9% (p<0.001); LDL:HDL ratio −26.2 ± 14.3% (p<0.001); triglycerides −16.3 ± 23.4% (p<0.05). No significant changes in the placebo group throughout the study.
limitations: Hypercholesterolaemic population only; specific insoluble polyphenol-rich fibre preparation not equivalent to standard dietary carob consumption; short 4-week duration

title: Commercial Carob Syrups in Randomised Controlled Trials: Effects on Lipid, Glycaemic, and Anthropometric Parameters (Planes-Munoz et al. 2025)
sample_size: Two complementary RCTs: (i) glycaemic test n=20; (ii) 6-week metabolic intervention n=72 (healthy adults aged 18-65)
finding: Both carob syrups: low glycaemic index (GI=56.04 and 60.46); postprandial glucose response attenuated by 16% vs glucose control (p<0.05). 6-week intervention: total cholesterol significantly reduced −14.68 ± 25.60 mg/dL (p<0.05); waist circumference reduced −3.58 ± 1.79 cm (p<0.05). Active compounds D-pinitol and polyphenols proposed as responsible mechanisms via insulin sensitisation and lipid metabolism modulation.
limitations: Healthy cohort; small to moderate effect sizes; commercially available syrup formulation may differ from whole carob pod or powder; authors describe findings as preliminary evidence

title: Effects of Pomegranate on Vascular Endothelial Function: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Clinical Trials (Kazemi et al. 2025)
sample_size: 19 clinical trials investigating effect of pomegranate on vascular endothelial function markers (ICAM-1, VCAM-1, IL-6, E-selectin, NO)
finding: IL-6 significantly reduced — pooled SMD −0.58 (95% CI −0.98 to −0.19, I²=82.6%) across 14 studies; ICAM-1 significantly reduced — SMD −0.63 (95% CI −0.85 to −0.40, I²=0%) across 3 studies; VCAM-1 non-significant; E-selectin inconsistent
limitations: High heterogeneity in IL-6 analysis (I²=82.6%); FMD and NO assessed in only one study each; predominantly Eastern countries studies

title: Effects of Pomegranate Juice on Blood Pressure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials (Sahebkar et al. 2016)
sample_size: 8 randomised placebo-controlled trials investigating pomegranate juice and blood pressure
finding: Pomegranate juice significantly reduced systolic BP: WMD −4.96 mmHg (95% CI −7.67 to −2.25; p<0.001); diastolic BP: WMD −2.01 mmHg (95% CI −3.71 to −0.31; p=0.021); SBP reduction robust across durations and doses in sensitivity analysis
limitations: Only 8 trials; dose-response relationship for DBP not fully characterised; SBP effect at doses >240cc showed borderline significance only for DBP

title: Efficacy of Artichoke Leaf Extract in Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease: A Pilot Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trial (Panahi et al. 2018)
sample_size: n=90 (NAFLD patients by ultrasound; double-blind placebo-controlled parallel; 2-month intervention; 49 ALE, 41 placebo)
finding: ALE 600mg/day vs placebo: hepatic vein flow increased (p<0.001); portal vein diameter and liver size reduced (p<0.001); ALT reduced (p<0.001); AST reduced (p<0.001); AST/ALT ratio and APRI score improved (p<0.01); total bilirubin reduced; total cholesterol, LDL, non-HDL, HDL, and TG all reduced (p=0.01)
limitations: Specific NAFLD population — results may not generalise to healthy adults; pilot study; 2-month duration; ALE supplement not equivalent to whole artichoke consumption

title: Impact of Phenolic-Rich Olive Leaf Extract on Blood Pressure, Plasma Lipids and Inflammatory Markers: A Randomised Controlled Trial (Lockyer et al. 2016)
sample_size: n=60 (pre-hypertensive males aged 45±12.7 years; double-blind randomised crossover; 6-week arms; 4-week washout)
finding: OLE (136mg oleuropein, 6mg hydroxytyrosol) vs polyphenol-free control: daytime SBP −3.95 mmHg (p=0.027); 24-h SBP −3.33 mmHg (p=0.045); daytime DBP −3.00 mmHg (p=0.025); 24-h DBP −2.42 mmHg (p=0.039); TC −0.32 mmol/L (p=0.002); LDL −0.19 mmol/L (p=0.017); TG −0.18 mmol/L (p=0.008); IL-8 −0.63 pg/mL (p=0.026)
limitations: Male-only sample; pre-hypertensive population only; crossover carries carryover risk despite washout; OLE concentration not equivalent to typical herbal tea preparation

title: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials of the Effect of Barley Beta-Glucan on LDL-C, Non-HDL-C and ApoB for CVD Risk Reduction (Ho et al. 2016)
sample_size: 14 randomised controlled trials; N=615 participants; median dose 6.5-6.9g/day; median duration 4 weeks
finding: Barley beta-glucan significantly reduced LDL-C: MD −0.25 mmol/L (95% CI −0.30 to −0.20); non-HDL-C: MD −0.31 mmol/L (95% CI −0.39 to −0.23); apoB not significantly changed; 3g/day sufficient for FDA cardiovascular health claim
limitations: Considerable unexplained heterogeneity in non-HDL-C (I²=98%); most trials short duration (4 weeks); varying food matrices; effects may differ by baseline cholesterol

title: Beta-Glucan from Barley and its Lipid-Lowering Capacity: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials (AbuMweis et al. 2010)
sample_size: 11 randomised clinical trials (1989-2008); multiple populations
finding: Barley and isolated beta-glucan lowered total cholesterol: WMD −0.30 mmol/L (95% CI −0.39 to −0.21; p<0.00001); LDL cholesterol: WMD −0.27 mmol/L (95% CI −0.34 to −0.20; p<0.00001) vs control; no dose-dependent response pattern; effects consistent across intervention type and food matrix
limitations: Older meta-analysis (up to 2008); no dose-response identified; heterogeneity in study designs

title: Impact of Probiotic Yogurt on Lipid Profiles in Subjects with Mild to Moderate Hypercholesterolaemia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Pourrajab et al. 2019)
sample_size: 7 randomised controlled trials; n=274 participants with mild to moderate hypercholesterolaemia; studies up to March 2019
finding: Probiotic yoghurt significantly reduced TC −8.73 mg/dL (95% CI −15.98 to −1.48; p=0.018) and LDL-C −10.61 mg/dL (95% CI −16.53 to −4.69; p<0.001) vs control; no significant change in HDL-C or triglycerides; low heterogeneity (I²=40.6% TC; I²=24.2% LDL) supporting consistency of the effect
limitations: Studies specifically in hypercholesterolaemic populations — effect in normocholesterolaemic individuals unclear; diverse probiotic strains across trials (L. acidophilus, L. rhamnosus, B. animalis, L. casei, L. fermentum); small total participant number (274); short intervention durations

title: Effects of Satureja Khuzestanica Supplementation on Glycaemic Indices and Lipid Profile in Type 2 Diabetes: A Randomised Controlled Clinical Trial (Roosta et al. 2024)
sample_size: Double-blind placebo-controlled RCT; n=78 T2DM patients (39 intervention, 39 placebo); 500mg SK capsules/day for 12 weeks — RELATED SPECIES to Cretan Satureja thymbra
finding: SK supplementation significantly reduced: FBS −12.6 vs +3.5 mg/dL (p=0.007); HbA1c −0.28 vs +0.11% (p<0.001); insulin −1.65 vs +2.09 mIU/L (p=0.03); TC −14.6 vs +8.2 mg/dL (p<0.001); LDL −4.6 vs +5.8 mg/dL (p<0.001); HDL +3.9 vs +0.9 mg/dL (p=0.005) — comprehensive metabolic improvement
limitations: Exclusively T2DM population — generalisability to healthy individuals unclear; study used Iranian species S. khuzestanica; Cretan S. thymbra shares carvacrol and thymol as dominant compounds but direct RCT evidence for the Cretan species is lacking; results should be extrapolated with caution

title: Efficacy of the Herbal Formula of Foeniculum vulgare and Rosa damascena on Elderly Patients with Functional Constipation: A Double-Blind Randomised Controlled Trial (Azimi et al. 2022)
sample_size: Double-blind randomised active-controlled trial; n=50 participants (25 per group); over-60 age group with functional constipation (Rome IV criteria); herbal formula vs PEG 4000 for 4 weeks with 4-week follow-up — NOTE: multi-herb formula; fennel is primary herb but Rosa damascena co-present
finding: Herbal formula group showed significantly greater improvement vs PEG 4000 in: constipation severity (p<0.001); stool consistency Bristol Scale (p<0.001); quality of life (p<0.001); longer duration of symptom relief; fewer side effects; both groups improved significantly vs baseline
limitations: Multi-herb formulation — cannot attribute effects to fennel alone; PEG 4000 comparator rather than true placebo; elderly population (over 60) only; mechanism of action described as unknown; conducted in Iran — may not be directly generalisable to Cretan varieties

title: Fermented Apulian Table Olives: Effect of Selected Microbial Starters on Polyphenols Composition, Antioxidant Activities and Bioaccessibility (D'Antuono et al. 2018)
sample_size: In vitro polyphenol characterisation and Caco-2 cell bioaccessibility assay; three Italian olive cultivars fermented with autochthonous microbial starters; NOTE: food-composition and bioaccessibility study — not a clinical intervention
finding: Fermented table olives contain hydroxytyrosol, tyrosol, verbascoside, and luteolin as primary phenolics; in BDC cultivar with starter, polyphenol content doubled vs commercial sample; bioaccessibility >60% for all phenolics by Caco-2 assay; HT and tyrosol are 8x more concentrated in table olive flesh than in olive oil; antioxidant capacity (CAA assay) highest in naturally fermented varieties
limitations: In vitro and ex vivo only — no human clinical outcomes measured; Italian olive cultivars (not Cretan Kolymvari); cardiovascular benefits extrapolated from bioavailability data and EVOO/hydroxytyrosol RCT evidence; clinical relevance depends on actual consumption amount and preparation method

title: Effect of Origanum vulgare Subsp. Essential Oils on Lipid Profiles and Liver Biomarkers in Athletes (Maral et al. 2021)
sample_size: RCT; n=34 trained athletes randomly assigned to 4 groups: O. v. subsp. dubium (DUB; 68% carvacrol), O. v. subsp. hirtum (HIR; 82.1% carvacrol), lavender (LAV), or control (CON); 14-day essential oil intervention — NOTE: O. v. subsp. hirtum is the Greek oregano subspecies with a carvacrol-dominant profile identical to Cretan rigani
finding: O. v. subsp. hirtum (HIR): HDL-C significantly higher than control (p=0.024); O. v. subsp. dubium (DUB): HDL-C increase (p=0.001) and LDL-C decrease (p=0.023) vs control; no significant changes in TC, TG, or liver biomarkers (AST, ALT, ALP, GGT) in any group; GC-MS confirmed 82.1% carvacrol in HIR oil and 68.0% in DUB
limitations: Very small n per group (~8–9 athletes per group); trained athlete population not generalisable to general public; EO supplement rather than dietary/culinary oregano; 14-day duration only; O. v. subsp. hirtum is the Greek oregano clade (carvacrol-dominant, as in Cretan rigani) but a direct Cretan-varietal dietary RCT is lacking; route of EO administration not fully specified

title: Three-Step Test System for the Identification of Novel GABA-A Receptor Modulating Food Plants (Sahin et al. 2016)
sample_size: In vitro GABA-A receptor expression system (Xenopus laevis oocytes); 10 aqueous food plant extracts screened by two-electrode voltage-clamp; GABA content quantified by HPLC-FLD to exclude endogenous-GABA artefacts; glycine receptor tested for specificity — NOTE: Sideritis sipylea tested; closely related to Cretan Malotira (S. syriaca / S. cretica)
finding: Sideritis sipylea was the second most potent specific GABA-A receptor modulator among all 10 food plants: potentiated GABA-induced current by 172 ± 19% at 0.5 µg/mL, second only to hops (Humulus lupulus, 182 ± 27%); effect confirmed GABA-specific — no cross-reactivity on glycine receptor; endogenous GABA content ruled out as artefact; hops is the most widely used plant-based sleep/sedation herb globally
limitations: In vitro receptor model only — no sleep outcome measured in humans or animals; Sideritis sipylea is a related but distinct species from Cretan Malotira (S. syriaca/S. cretica); oocyte GABA-A potentiation may not translate to clinical sedative effect at dietary tea doses; mechanism validates traditional sedative use but clinical confirmation is lacking

title: Purslane: A Plant Source of Omega-3 Fatty Acids and Melatonin (Simopoulos et al. 2005)
sample_size: Phytochemical composition analysis; GC/MS quantification of melatonin in Portulaca oleracea leaves; published in Journal of Pineal Research by Russel J. Reiter's group (world's leading melatonin researchers); cross-confirmed at 19 ng/g WW in Zhao et al. 2017 dietary melatonin review (PMC5409706)
finding: Purslane leaves contain 19 ng/g wet weight melatonin by GC/MS — the highest melatonin concentration reported among commonly consumed vegetables; 13x higher than ginger (1.42 ng/g WW), 63x higher than tomato (0.30 ng/g WW), 475x higher than spinach (0.04 ng/g WW); purslane also contains omega-3 ALA as the dominant fatty acid — the only land plant with nutritionally significant levels of both melatonin and omega-3
limitations: Composition study only — no human sleep outcome measured; dietary melatonin from food must survive gastric digestion and cross the blood-brain barrier to exert sleep effects; concentrations in food are lower than the 0.5–5 mg pharmacological doses used in clinical sleep RCTs; no human RCT has tested purslane specifically for sleep; Cretan wild purslane (glistrida) vs. cultivated varieties not compared — melatonin content may vary by cultivar, season, and light exposure

title: Consumption of Olive Oil and Risk of Total and Cause-Specific Mortality Among U.S. Adults (Guasch-Ferré et al. 2022)
sample_size: n=92,383 (60,582 women NHS + 31,801 men HPFS; 28-year follow-up; 36,856 deaths)
finding: Highest olive oil consumption (>0.5 tbsp/day or >7 g/d) vs never/rarely: all-cause mortality HR 0.81 (95% CI 0.78–0.84); CVD mortality HR 0.81 (0.75–0.87, −19%); cancer mortality HR 0.83 (0.78–0.89, −17%); neurodegenerative disease mortality HR 0.71 (0.64–0.78, −29%); respiratory disease mortality HR 0.82 (0.72–0.93, −18%). Substitution analysis: replacing 10 g/d of margarine, butter, mayonnaise, or dairy fat with olive oil was associated with 8–34% lower risk of total and cause-specific mortality.
limitations: Observational design — cannot establish causation; self-reported FFQ; cohort predominantly US health professionals; EVOO vs standard olive oil not always distinguished; no significant difference vs other vegetable oils when directly compared
health_goal_tags: Longevity & ageing; Cardiovascular health; Mental clarity & stress; Inflammation & immunity

title: Effect of Olive Oil Consumption on Cardiovascular Disease, Cancer, Type 2 Diabetes, and All-Cause Mortality: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis (Martinez-Gonzalez et al. 2022)
sample_size: 36 studies; 24 prospective cohorts + 1 RCT (PREDIMED); 733,420 participants with 174,081 deaths; 806,203 with 49,223 CVD events; 680,239 with 13,389 T2D cases
finding: Per 25 g/day increment in olive oil consumption: all-cause mortality RR 0.89 (95% CI 0.85–0.93); CVD RR 0.84 (0.76–0.94, −16%); type 2 diabetes RR 0.78 (0.69–0.87, −22% — homogeneous across studies); cancer RR 0.94 (0.86–1.03, not significant). Effects consistent across cohorts following participants 3.7 to 28 years.
limitations: Most evidence observational (24/27 quantitative studies); heterogeneity in cardiovascular and mortality outcomes; PREDIMED is the only RCT and used MedDiet+EVOO arm rather than EVOO alone; FFQ-based dietary assessment
health_goal_tags: Longevity & ageing; Cardiovascular health; Energy & metabolism

title: Olive Oil Consumption and Risk of Cardiovascular Disease and All-Cause Mortality: Meta-Analysis of Prospective Cohort Studies (Xia et al. 2022)
sample_size: 13 prospective cohorts
finding: Highest vs lowest olive oil consumption: CVD RR 0.85 (95% CI 0.77–0.93, p<0.001); all-cause mortality RR 0.83 (0.77–0.90, p<0.001). Dose-response per 5 g/day: CVD RR 0.96 (0.93–0.99); all-cause mortality RR 0.96 (0.95–0.96). Non-linear association: little additional risk reduction observed beyond approximately 20 g/day.
limitations: All studies observational; substantial heterogeneity; non-linear plateau beyond ~20 g/day means pharmacological-level doses are not warranted; type of olive oil (EVOO vs refined) not always specified

title: Plasma free amino acid profile in quiescent Inflammatory Bowel Disease patients orally administered Mastiha (Pistacia lentiscus): randomised clinical trial (Papada et al. 2018)
sample_size: n=68 (IBD patients in remission; double-blind placebo-controlled; 6 months)
finding: Mastiha 2.8 g/day: attenuated the increase in plasma free amino acids that occurs prior to IBD relapse — alanine (p=0.006), valine (p=0.047), proline (p=0.022), glutamine (p<0.001), and tyrosine (p=0.043) all rose significantly in the placebo group but not in the mastiha group; total cholesterol (p=0.032) and LDL cholesterol (p=0.045) also rose only in placebo. Serum IL-6, faecal calprotectin, and faecal lactoferrin increased only in placebo group. Although clinical relapse rates did not differ significantly (17.6% vs 23.5%), the inflammatory and metabolic biomarker pattern strongly favoured mastiha.
limitations: Clinical relapse rate non-significant (study underpowered for hard clinical endpoint); IBD-specific population; mechanism described as remission maintenance rather than active disease treatment; Pistacia lentiscus var. chia specifically (Chios mastic) — Cretan-grown Pistacia lentiscus may have similar but not identical phytochemistry

title: Real-world safety and effectiveness of Pistacia lentiscus (mastic gum) in patients with diabetic gastroparesis: 24-week interim analysis (Kant et al. 2024)
sample_size: n=38 (diabetic gastroparesis; double-blind randomised; 24-week follow-up)
finding: Mastic gum vs levosulpiride (standard prokinetic drug): mean change in Gastrointestinal Cardinal Symptom Index (GCSI) at 24 weeks was statistically significantly different between groups (p<0.001), with mastic gum demonstrating sustainable symptom improvement. Within the mastic gum arm, GCSI improvement at 24 weeks (16.7±3.81) was non-inferior to the 2-month post-intervention score (16.35±2.27, p=0.89), indicating durable benefit without obvious adverse effects.
limitations: Small sample size (n=38); diabetic gastroparesis-specific population — generalisability to functional dyspepsia or general GI complaints requires extrapolation; non-inferiority comparison rather than placebo-controlled; single-centre Indian study

title: The effect of Chios mastic toothpaste on halitosis and oral hygiene in orthodontic patients: a randomized clinical trial (Alexiou et al. 2025)
sample_size: n=32 (adolescents with fixed orthodontic appliances; double-blind placebo-controlled parallel group; 14 days)
finding: Mastic toothpaste used 3x daily for 14 days: hydrogen sulfide breath levels reduced from 158 ppb to 26 ppb (p=0.001); Gingival Index reduced from 1.8 to 1.0 (p<0.001); Modified Plaque Index reduced from 1.2 to 0.8 (p<0.001) — clinically meaningful reductions in plaque, gingival inflammation, and oral malodour vs placebo. Mechanism: mastic triterpenic acids and alpha-pinene have documented antimicrobial activity against oral pathogens including S. mutans and P. gingivalis.
limitations: Topical oral application (toothpaste) not equivalent to dietary mastic consumption; small n=32 sample; short 14-day duration; orthodontic patient population; secondary outcomes (dimethyl sulfide, methyl-mercaptan) did not differ between groups

title: Capparis spinosa L. (Caper) fruit extract in treatment of type 2 diabetic patients: randomized double-blind placebo-controlled clinical trial (Huseini et al. 2013)
sample_size: n=54 (T2DM patients on standard anti-diabetic therapy; 2 months; 400mg caper fruit extract 3x daily)
finding: Caper fruit extract (1200mg/day) significantly reduced fasting blood glucose (p=0.037) and HbA1c (p=0.043) vs placebo at 2 months in T2DM patients already on standard oral hypoglycaemic therapy. Triglycerides also decreased significantly within the caper group from baseline (p=0.29). No liver, kidney, or other adverse effects observed across the 2-month intervention.
limitations: T2DM-specific population already on hypoglycaemic medications; relatively small n=54; 2-month duration; capsule-formulation extract not equivalent to dietary salt-cured caper consumption; mechanism attributed to quercetin and rutin without direct mechanistic confirmation
health_goal_tags: Energy & metabolism; Blood sugar & metabolic balance

title: Effect of Capparis spinosa Extract on Metabolic Parameters in Patients with Type-2 Diabetes: Randomized Controlled Trial (Vahid et al. 2019)
sample_size: n=30 (poorly controlled T2DM with metabolic syndrome; triple-blind placebo-controlled; 3 months; oxymel formulation)
finding: C. spinosa oxymel (10 mL × 3 daily): inhibited the progression of hyperglycaemia — fasting blood glucose and postprandial blood glucose levels continued rising in placebo and simple oxymel groups but did not progress in C. spinosa oxymel group. Inhibited progression of hypertriglyceridaemia; significantly reduced body weight and BMI from baseline. No significant effect on HbA1c or serum cholesterol; no hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, or other adverse effects observed.
limitations: Small sample n=30 across 3 arms (10 each); poorly controlled T2DM population already on multiple medications; oxymel formulation combines vinegar + caper extract — caper-specific effect not fully isolatable; results do not show improvement, only attenuation of further deterioration
health_goal_tags: Energy & metabolism; Blood sugar & metabolic balance

title: Effect of caper fruit (Capparis spinosa L.) consumption on liver enzymes, lipid profile, fasting plasma glucose, and weight loss: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Perna et al. 2023)
sample_size: 5 RCTs (n=178 adults across NAFLD; T2DM; metabolic syndrome; hyperlipidaemia; 2-12 week interventions)
finding: Caper fruit consumption significantly improved: alanine aminotransferase (ALT) −12.29 U/L (95% CI −24.47 to −0.11); HDL cholesterol +0.72 mg/dL (95% CI 0.10 to 1.34); body weight −1.00 kg (95% CI −1.44 to −0.56). Trends toward improvement (non-significant) for AST, triglycerides, LDL, total cholesterol, and fasting plasma glucose. Caper supports the liver–lipid axis in patients with metabolic syndrome and diabetes.
limitations: Only 5 RCTs available (n=178 total); short to medium intervention duration (2-12 weeks); diverse populations and caper preparations (capsule extract, oxymel, dry fruit) — heterogeneity limits firm conclusions; authors note paucity of data on this topic

title: Effects of walnut consumption on blood lipids and other cardiovascular risk factors: updated meta-analysis and systematic review of controlled trials (Guasch-Ferré et al. 2018)
sample_size: 26 controlled trials with 1059 participants
finding: Walnut-enriched diets vs control: total cholesterol WMD −6.99 mg/dL (95% CI −9.39 to −4.58; p<0.001) — 3.25% greater reduction; LDL cholesterol WMD −5.51 mg/dL (95% CI −7.72 to −3.29; p<0.001) — 3.73% greater reduction; triglycerides WMD −4.69 mg/dL (95% CI −8.93 to −0.45; p=0.03) — 5.52% greater reduction; apolipoprotein B (the protein on every LDL particle, a strong CVD risk marker) WMD −3.74 mg/dL (95% CI −6.51 to −0.97; p=0.008). Effects more pronounced vs American/Western diet controls (TC −12.3 mg/dL). No significant impact on body weight or blood pressure — walnuts deliver cardiovascular benefit without weight gain despite high energy density.
limitations: Heterogeneous control diets across 26 trials; dose and walnut form varied; most studies short-term; effects most pronounced in participants already consuming Western/American diets

title: The effect of walnut consumption on cardiometabolic profiles of individuals with abnormal glucose homeostasis: systematic review and meta-analysis (Malmir et al. 2021)
sample_size: 8 trials in adults with abnormal glucose homeostasis (pre-diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance)
finding: Walnut supplementation significantly improved flow-mediated dilation (FMD — the gold-standard non-invasive measure of endothelial function) by 0.93% (95% CI 0.16 to 1.71); LDL cholesterol trended lower −0.10 mmol/L (95% CI −0.20 to 0.01; p=0.06). No significant effect on body weight, BMI, waist circumference, fasting glucose, HbA1c, blood pressure, or other lipid markers in this specific pre-diabetic / IGT population. FMD improvement reflects walnut alpha-linolenic acid and arginine-mediated NO pathway enhancement.
limitations: Specific pre-diabetic/IGT population — not a generalisable insulin-resistance benefit; only 8 trials in meta-analysis; no significant effect on most glycaemic markers; FMD as a surrogate endpoint

title: Almond Consumption and Risk Factors for Cardiovascular Disease: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials (Lee-Bravatti et al. 2019)
sample_size: 15 RCTs with 534 subjects (adults healthy or at CVD risk; trials ≥3 weeks; ~42.5g/day target dose)
finding: Almond intervention significantly improved: total cholesterol −10.69 mg/dL (95% CI −16.75 to −4.63); LDL cholesterol −5.83 mg/dL (95% CI −9.91 to −1.75); body weight −1.39 kg (95% CI −2.49 to −0.30); HDL cholesterol −1.26 mg/dL (95% CI −2.47 to −0.05); apolipoprotein B −6.67 mg/dL (95% CI −12.63 to −0.72). At doses >42.5 g/day specifically: fasting blood glucose, diastolic blood pressure, and BMI also significantly reduced. No significant change in triglycerides, systolic BP, hsCRP, or lipoprotein(a). Almonds reduce CVD risk via improved lipid profile and body weight without compensatory adverse effects.
limitations: Heterogeneous control diets and almond doses; most trials short to medium duration; HDL also decreased (slight) — interpretation requires considering total-to-HDL ratio rather than HDL alone; dose-response effect for glucose and BP only seen at >42.5 g/day

title: The effects of almond consumption on fasting blood lipid levels: systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Musa-Veloso et al. 2016)
sample_size: 18 publications with 27 almond-control datasets
finding: Almond consumption significantly reduced total cholesterol −0.153 mmol/L (p<0.001); LDL cholesterol −0.124 mmol/L (p=0.001); triglycerides −0.067 mmol/L (p=0.042); HDL cholesterol not significantly affected (−0.017 mmol/L; p=0.207) — preserving the protective HDL pool while reducing atherogenic LDL. Results align with prospective cohort data linking nut consumption to reduced heart disease risk.
limitations: Older meta-analysis (data through ~2015); heterogeneity in almond doses and forms (whole, ground, almond butter, skin-on vs blanched); short-to-medium term trials predominantly

title: The Acute and Chronic Cognitive Effects of a Sage Extract: Randomized Placebo-Controlled Study in Healthy Humans (Wightman et al. 2021)
sample_size: n=94 healthy adults (30-60 years; double-blind randomised parallel group; 29 days; 600 mg/day Cognivia sage extract)
finding: Sage extract (combination of Salvia officinalis polyphenols + Salvia lavandulaefolia terpenoids) significantly improved working memory and accuracy across multiple cognitive tasks — Corsi Blocks (spatial working memory), Numeric Working Memory, and Name-to-Face Recall — both acutely (within day 1 and day 29) and chronically (across the 29-day intervention). Effects observed at 120- and 240-min post-dose. Mechanism: sage polyphenols (rosmarinic acid, carnosic acid) and terpenes (1,8-cineole, alpha-thujone) inhibit acetylcholinesterase — the same target as Alzheimer disease drugs donepezil and rivastigmine.
limitations: Single proprietary combination extract — not directly equivalent to traditional Cretan faskomilo herbal infusion; Salvia officinalis and S. lavandulaefolia studied — Cretan S. fruticosa shares carnosic acid, rosmarinic acid, and 1,8-cineole but has a distinct chemotype with higher 1,8-cineole and beta-thujone; healthy adults only — not tested in MCI or dementia populations

title: Systematic review of clinical trials assessing pharmacological properties of Salvia species on memory, cognitive impairment, and Alzheimers disease (Miroddi et al. 2014)
sample_size: 14 clinical studies of Salvia officinalis and Salvia lavandulaefolia (related Salvia species)
finding: Salvia officinalis and S. lavandulaefolia significantly enhanced cognitive performance in both healthy subjects (acute attention and memory improvements) and patients with mild-to-moderate Alzheimers disease (cognitive scale improvements). Mechanism converges on acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase inhibition by 1,8-cineole, alpha-thujone, and rosmarinic acid — the same enzymes targeted by prescription Alzheimers drugs. Sage species are well-tolerated; no serious adverse events reported across reviewed trials.
limitations: Authors note methodological heterogeneity across reviewed trials (different sage preparations: dried herb, essential oil, hydroalcoholic extract); studies use S. officinalis and S. lavandulaefolia — Cretan S. fruticosa is a different species with overlapping but distinct chemotype; small individual trial sample sizes

title: The effect of pomegranate juice supplementation on C-reactive protein levels: GRADE-assessed systematic review and dose-response updated meta-analysis (Jazinaki et al. 2024)
sample_size: 11 RCTs (13 effect sizes; 696 participants); adults supplemented with pomegranate juice vs control
finding: PJ supplementation significantly reduced CRP: WMD −2.55 mg/L (95% CI −3.44 to −1.66; p<0.001); subgroup effects confirmed in females, T2D and PCOS populations; nonsignificant linear dose-response
limitations: Subgroup effects limit generalisability to broader populations; optimal dose and duration not established; heterogeneity not fully characterised; more RCTs recommended

title: Crithmum maritimum L.: Phytochemical Profile, Biological Activities, and Therapeutic Potential (Dzhoglova et al. 2025)
sample_size: Narrative review of 79 in vitro and in vivo studies on Crithmum maritimum
finding: Essential oil components show in vitro antibacterial, antifungal, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anticancer activity; extracts exhibit hypoglycaemic, vasodilatory, and prebiotic effects in preclinical models; cholinesterase inhibition suggests cognitive potential
limitations: No human clinical trials; all evidence from in vitro and animal studies; number of experimental studies described as limited; clinical translation not yet established

title: Nutritive Value and Bioactivities of a Halophyte Edible Plant: Crithmum maritimum L. (Correia et al. 2024)
sample_size: Compositional and bioactivity analysis of sea fennel leaves, flowers, and schizocarps; Caco-2 intestinal model for prebiotic assessment
finding: Rich in omega-6/omega-3 PUFAs (linoleic acid dominant); high polyphenol and antioxidant content in flowers and schizocarps; antimicrobial against common pathogens; prebiotic effect on Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium in Caco-2 model; non-toxic up to 1.0%
limitations: In vitro / compositional study; no human clinical data; Caco-2 is a cell model, not a human gut microbiome trial

title: Physicochemistry, Nutritional, and Therapeutic Potential of Ficus carica — A Promising Nutraceutical (Fazel et al. 2024)
sample_size: Narrative review of 126 studies on Ficus carica published 1999–2023; databases: PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus, Google Scholar
finding: Fig extracts demonstrate antioxidant, anti-neurodegenerative, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, anti-arthritic, antidiabetic, and anticonvulsant properties in preclinical models; anthocyanins inhibit cholinesterase potentially protective in Alzheimer's disease; antimicrobial activity via flavonoids and terpenoids; generally low toxicity profile
limitations: All evidence from preclinical (in vitro and animal) studies; authors note 'more research required specifically on safety, efficacy, and clinical trials'; no human RCTs on whole fig consumption identified
health_goal_tags: Inflammation & immunity;Blood sugar & metabolic balance;Longevity & ageing

title: Nutritional Composition, Fatty Acids Profile, Mineral Content, Antioxidant Activity and Acute Toxicity of the Flesh of H. aspersa Müller (Aouji et al. 2023)
sample_size: Chemical analysis of H. aspersa flesh: proximate composition, fatty acid profile, minerals, antioxidant capacity (DPPH), and acute toxicity in laboratory rats
finding: Good omega-3/omega-6 ratio; predominantly unsaturated fatty acids; high antioxidant capacity; ~77 kcal per 100g; LD50 >2000 mg/kg body weight (safe); consumption highly recommended due to nutrient density and unsaturated fat profile
limitations: Compositional study only; no human clinical data; antioxidant activity measured in vitro; single species and population; safety established by acute toxicity study in rats, not human trials

title: Helix aspersa flour: An evaluation for dietary supplementation (Bongiorno et al. 2024)
sample_size: Nutritional and safety analysis of snail flour from H. aspersa aspersa: moisture, ash, protein, fat, essential amino acids, PUFAs, heavy metals, PAHs, PCBs, PBDEs
finding: Notable presence of polyunsaturated fatty acids and essential amino acids; heavy metal concentrations on par with or lower than literature values; PAHs, PCBs and PBDEs below detectable limits; supports use as sustainable protein source
limitations: Snail flour product rather than whole cooked flesh; compositional data only; no clinical outcomes assessed; sustainable protein framing focused on food security rather than therapeutic claims

title: Efficacy and tolerability of a red-vine-leaf extract in patients suffering from chronic venous insufficiency — results of a double-blind placebo-controlled study
sample_size: 248 (CVI patients CEAP 3-4a)
finding: Red vine leaf extract AS195 720 mg/day for 12 weeks reduced lower leg volume by 19.9 mL vs placebo (p=0.0268) and reduced leg pain on VAS by 6.6 mm vs placebo (p=0.047); tolerability comparable to placebo.
limitations: Uses standardised concentrated AS195 (Antistax) extract, not whole vine leaves consumed in dolmadakia; extrapolation to dietary intake assumes shared quercetin glycoside bioactives at lower concentrations.

title: The role of venoactive compounds in the treatment of chronic venous disease
sample_size: not applicable
finding: Comprehensive 2025 review of venoactive compounds applying GRADE methodology; red vine leaf extract included among compounds with evidence-supported efficacy in chronic venous disease symptom relief (pain, cramps, heaviness) and edema reduction.
limitations: Reviews concentrated extracts not whole-food intake; quality grading is for the extract not for vine leaves as eaten.

title: Valorization of grape leaves for bioactive compounds: novel green extraction technologies and food-pharma applications
sample_size: not applicable
finding: Review of grape leaf phytochemistry identifies quercetin, resveratrol, caffeic acid, kaempferol, and gallic acid as primary bioactives; documents antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-obesity, anti-diabetic, and hepatoprotective effects across in vitro and animal studies.
limitations: Composition and mechanism review; does not establish dose-response in humans for whole-leaf consumption.

title: Thymol, thyme, and other plant sources: Health and potential uses
sample_size: not applicable
finding: Comprehensive review of thymol bioactivities: documented antimicrobial, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticarcinogenesis, antispasmodic, expectorant, and respiratory tract effects; thymol is 10-64% of thyme essential oil; long-standing clinical use in expectorant cough formulations.
limitations: Compositional and pharmacological review; whole-leaf consumption dose-response in humans is not the primary focus.

title: Thymol and Thyme Essential Oil — New Insights into Selected Therapeutic Applications
sample_size: not applicable
finding: Therapeutic review: thyme essential oil and thymol with documented expectorant, anti-inflammatory, antiviral, antibacterial, and antiseptic activity; emerging evidence for antibiofilm, antifungal, and antileishmanial applications; new nano-encapsulated formulations under investigation.
limitations: Review covers concentrated essential oil — culinary thyme use delivers far smaller doses of thymol and carvacrol than therapeutic preparations.

title: Meta-analysis of the antifungal activities of three essential oils as alternative therapies in dermatophytosis infections
sample_size: 54 studies
finding: Thymus vulgaris essential oil demonstrated the lowest minimum fungicidal concentration (MFC=4.2 μl/ml) against Trichophyton rubrum among the three essential oils analysed; positions thyme as a candidate antifungal where conventional treatments fail.
limitations: In vitro meta-analysis; clinical efficacy in human dermatophytosis remains to be confirmed in well-powered RCTs.

title: Trace elements, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, mineral composition, and FT-IR characterization of unrefined sea and rock salts: environmental interactions
sample_size: 24 Greek sea and rock salt samples
finding: Characterised the mineral composition of Greek unrefined sea salts and rock salts; detected measurable trace metals (Cd, Co, Cr, Cu, Fe, Mn, Ni, Pb, Zn) and PAHs; quite high lead values found in both sea and rock salts compared to typical seawater concentrations.
limitations: Compositional analysis of retail samples; does not directly assess clinical health outcomes from sea salt consumption.

title: Assessment of trace element contamination and human health risk in unrefined sea salt from Chattogram and Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh
sample_size: 40 unrefined sea salt samples
finding: All measured trace elements (Cr, Cd, Pb, Fe, As, Ni) exceeded FAO/WHO safety limits; cumulative non-carcinogenic hazard index >1.0 across all regions; carcinogenic risk for Cd, As, and Cr surpassed acceptable threshold (1.0E-04) — strong evidence that "unrefined sea salt" is not automatically safer than refined.
limitations: Bangladesh-specific samples; trace metal load varies regionally with coastal pollution — Greek and Cretan sources may differ but not assumed contaminant-free (see Karavoltsos 2020).

title: Novel Probiotic Candidates in Artisanal Feta-Type Kefalonian Cheese
sample_size: not applicable
finding: Lpb. plantarum F89/F162/F254 and Lcb. paracasei F214/F216 isolated from Greek feta-type cheese; demonstrated cholesterol assimilation, alpha-glucosidase inhibition, and Caco-2 epithelial adhesion; identified as candidate probiotic strains
limitations: Artisanal Kefalonian feta only; all results in vitro; no clinical intervention

title: Characterization of Bacterial Microbiota of P.D.O. Feta Cheese by 16S Metagenomic Analysis
sample_size: not applicable
finding: PDO feta harbours 59 bacterial species across 5 phyla; Streptococcaceae and Lactobacillaceae dominant families; 21 nonstarter LAB strains identified; distinct regional microbiota fingerprints
limitations: Descriptive microbiota characterisation only; no clinical health outcomes measured

title: Fish consumption and multiple health outcomes: umbrella review of 91 meta-analyses
sample_size: 91 meta-analyses included
finding: 17 beneficial associations with moderate/high evidence quality: all-cause mortality, CVD mortality, IBD, metabolic syndrome, AMD, multiple sclerosis among others; 1-2 servings fatty fish/week appears safe and protective
limitations: Umbrella review; fish type not always distinguished; predominantly observational evidence
health_goal_tags: Cardiovascular health / Longevity & ageing / Inflammation & immunity

title: Intake of fish and marine n-3 PUFA and risk of cardiovascular disease mortality: meta-analysis of 25 prospective cohort studies
finding: Fish consumption inversely associated with CVD mortality (RR=0.91, 95% CI 0.85-0.98); n-3 PUFA intake: RR=0.87 (95% CI 0.85-0.89) for CVD mortality; 4% CVD mortality reduction per additional 20g fish/day
limitations: Cohort studies; fish type not specified; residual confounding possible

title: Determination of imidazole dipeptides and taurine in natural seafoods by LC-MS/MS
sample_size: not applicable
finding: Boiled octopus among the highest taurine-containing seafoods quantified; taurine most abundant in squid, boiled octopus, and scallop; provides compositional basis for taurine health claims
limitations: Compositional analysis only; no human health outcomes measured

title: Protective effects of octopus hydrolysate against oxidative stress in liver cells and zebrafish
sample_size: not applicable
finding: Alcalase hydrolysate of Octopus ocellatus meat reduced ROS in human hepatocytes; high taurine content confirmed; DPPH and ABTS radical scavenging; improved survival in zebrafish embryo model
limitations: In vitro and zebrafish model only; hydrolysate not equivalent to whole food consumption; no human data

title: Nutritional composition, health benefits and claim conditions of Sparus aurata and Dicentrarchus labrax: narrative review
sample_size: not applicable
finding: Both species provide EU-authorised health claim-qualifying omega-3, protein, selenium, and phosphorus; regular consumption supports cardiovascular, cognitive, and visual health; anti-inflammatory effects documented; farmed fish nutritionally equivalent to wild-caught
limitations: Narrative review; farmed fish omega-3 content varies with feed composition; no primary RCT data
health_goal_tags: Cardiovascular health / Inflammation & immunity / Mental clarity & stress

title: Saffron (Crocus sativus) in neurological and psychiatric disorders: systematic review and meta-analysis of 46 RCTs
sample_size: 46 RCTs included
finding: Saffron superior to placebo: depression effect size -4.26 (95% CI -5.76 to -2.77); anxiety -3.75 (95% CI -5.83 to -1.67); sleep disorders -1.91 (95% CI -2.88 to -0.93); non-inferior to conventional drugs for depression, anxiety, ADHD, OCD; well tolerated
limitations: Predominantly short trials (4-48 weeks); dosing varies across studies; publication bias possible in positive trials

title: Plant-based medicines in psychiatric disorders: meta-review of RCT meta-analyses
sample_size: 5927 (9 meta-analyses)
finding: Saffron identified as one of three phytoceuticals with meta-analytic support for major depressive disorder, alongside St John's wort and curcumin; effect sizes for depression and anxiety significant across multiple reviews
limitations: Possible publication bias in included meta-analyses; methodological quality variable

title: Physicochemical characterization and biological properties of pine honey produced across Greece
sample_size: not applicable
finding: Greek pine honey: total phenolics 451±120 mg GAE/kg; FRAP 1.87-9.43 mmol Fe/kg (higher than most European honeys); antibacterial MIC values comparable or superior to Manuka honey against 5 nosocomial and foodborne pathogens including S. aureus and S. Typhimurium; multiple mechanisms of antibacterial action confirmed
limitations: In vitro only; antibacterial activity does not directly translate to clinical outcomes; pine honey composition varies by region and season

title: Glycemic index and appetite response of iron-biofortified cowpeas in healthy adults
finding: All cowpea varieties produced significantly lower incremental AUC than glucose; Pajeu variety showed lowest hunger and highest satiety sensation (p<0.05); biofortified cowpeas reduced NF-κB translocation in RAW 264.7 macrophages; anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects confirmed in cell model
limitations: Small sample (n=11); single acute feeding study; Brazilian varieties, not Greek cultivars; anti-inflammatory data from cell model only
health_goal_tags: Blood sugar & metabolic balance / Inflammation & immunity
